warmup.q: A codebase evaluates expressions with a classic Visitor: ExprVisitor with visitNum, visitAdd, visitMul, and four visitor classes. You add a fifth node type, Neg. What do you have to touch?
options: The visitor interface, an accept on Neg, and all four visitor classes
Nothing: the visitor finds Neg through reflection
warmup.why: Visitor makes new operations cheap (a new visitor class) and new cases expensive: every visitor must learn the new case, and the interface needs a visitNeg. That is one half of the expression problem. A sealed type with switch has the same trade-off, but the compiler lists every place to change.

sections.h: Visitor, the expression problem, and sealed types
sections.html:
Visitor lets you add operations to a fixed set of classes without editing those classes. Here is the classic form, for a tiny expression tree:

Java
interface ExprVisitor<R> { R visitNum(Num n); R visitAdd(Add a); R visitMul(Mul m); }

sealed interface Expr permits Num, Add, Mul { <R> R accept(ExprVisitor<R> v); }
record Num(int value) implements Expr { public <R> R accept(ExprVisitor<R> v) { return v.visitNum(this); } }
record Add(Expr l, Expr r) implements Expr { public <R> R accept(ExprVisitor<R> v) { return v.visitAdd(this); } }
record Mul(Expr l, Expr r) implements Expr { public <R> R accept(ExprVisitor<R> v) { return v.visitMul(this); } }

final class Eval implements ExprVisitor<Integer> {
    public Integer visitNum(Num n) { return n.value(); }
    public Integer visitAdd(Add a) { return a.l().accept(this) + a.r().accept(this); }
    public Integer visitMul(Mul m) { return m.l().accept(this) * m.r().accept(this); }
}

int result = expr.accept(new Eval());      // double dispatch: accept picks the case, visit picks the operation
Kotlin
interface ExprVisitor<R> { fun visitNum(n: Num): R; fun visitAdd(a: Add): R; fun visitMul(m: Mul): R }

sealed interface Expr { fun <R> accept(v: ExprVisitor<R>): R }
data class Num(val value: Int) : Expr { override fun <R> accept(v: ExprVisitor<R>) = v.visitNum(this) }
data class Add(val l: Expr, val r: Expr) : Expr { override fun <R> accept(v: ExprVisitor<R>) = v.visitAdd(this) }
data class Mul(val l: Expr, val r: Expr) : Expr { override fun <R> accept(v: ExprVisitor<R>) = v.visitMul(this) }

object Eval : ExprVisitor<Int> {
    override fun visitNum(n: Num) = n.value
    override fun visitAdd(a: Add) = a.l.accept(this) + a.r.accept(this)
    override fun visitMul(m: Mul) = m.l.accept(this) * m.r.accept(this)
}

val result = expr.accept(Eval)             // double dispatch: accept picks the case, visit picks the operation

A new operation, such as printing, is one new visitor class. A new case, Neg, costs a method on the visitor interface, an accept on Neg, and an edit in every visitor anyone ever wrote.

That trade-off is the expression problem. With ordinary virtual methods (an eval() on each record), a new case is cheap and a new operation touches every class. With Visitor it's the other way round. Plain Java and Kotlin can't make both cheap, so you pick the axis you expect to grow.

In payment code, the axis that grows is usually operations. The instruction types (card, SEPA transfer, wallet payout) change rarely, while new validations, exports, reports and fee rules arrive all the time. That favors Visitor's side of the trade.

Sealed types and pattern matching give you Visitor's side of the trade without its machinery: no accept, no visitor interface, one function per operation with a switch or when inside. The comparison below shows it in both languages. Brian Goetz puts it bluntly in the pattern-matching design notes: "if your language has sufficiently powerful pattern matching, the Visitor pattern is almost completely unnecessary". The same notes say this doesn't make virtual methods wrong.

So, for a closed hierarchy you own, delete the visitor. Keep Visitor when the hierarchy is open across modules, or when a library hands you one: javax.lang.model.element.ElementVisitor in annotation processors, javac's Tree API, ASM's ClassVisitor.

try.title: Add a case in both styles
steps: Run VisitorVsSwitch (Java or Kotlin) and check both results agree.

Add a Neg case. Java: add Neg to permits and record Neg(Expr e) implements Expr { public <R> R accept(ExprVisitor<R> v) { return v.visitNeg(this); } }. Kotlin: data class Neg(val e: Expr) : Expr { override fun <R> accept(v: ExprVisitor<R>) = v.visitNeg(this) }. Build with the demo command.
Fix each error the compiler gives you, build again, and keep a count of the places you edited.

code.title: VisitorVsSwitch.java
code.html: package workbench.patterns.l10; /** The same expression tree evaluated with a classic Visitor and with a sealed switch. */ public class VisitorVsSwitch { interface ExprVisitor<R> { R visitNum(Num n); R visitAdd(Add a); R visitMul(Mul m); } sealed interface Expr permits Num, Add, Mul { <R> R accept(ExprVisitor<R> v); } record Num(int value) implements Expr { public <R> R accept(ExprVisitor<R> v) { return v.visitNum(this); } } record Add(Expr l, Expr r) implements Expr { public <R> R accept(ExprVisitor<R> v) { return v.visitAdd(this); } } record Mul(Expr l, Expr r) implements Expr { public <R> R accept(ExprVisitor<R> v) { return v.visitMul(this); } } // operation 1, visitor style: one class per operation, one method per case static final class Eval implements ExprVisitor<Integer> { public Integer visitNum(Num n) { return n.value(); } public Integer visitAdd(Add a) { return a.l().accept(this) + a.r().accept(this); } public Integer visitMul(Mul m) { return m.l().accept(this) * m.r().accept(this); } } // operation 1 again, data style: no accept needed, no visitor interface static int eval(Expr e) { return switch (e) { case Num(var v) -> v; case Add(var l, var r) -> eval(l) + eval(r); case Mul(Num(var z), var r) when z == 0 -> 0; // nested record pattern: hard to say with a visitor case Mul(var l, var r) -> eval(l) * eval(r); }; } // operation 2: just one more function static String show(Expr e) { return switch (e) { case Num(var v) -> Integer.toString(v); case Add(var l, var r) -> "(" + show(l) + " + " + show(r) + ")"; case Mul(var l, var r) -> show(l) + " * " + show(r); }; } public static void main(String[] args) { Expr e = new Add(new Num(2), new Mul(new Num(3), new Num(4))); System.out.println(show(e) + " = " + e.accept(new Eval()) + " (visitor) = " + eval(e) + " (switch)"); Expr zero = new Mul(new Num(0), e); System.out.println(show(zero) + " = " + eval(zero)); } }

alt.title: VisitorVsSwitch.kt
alt.html: package workbench.patterns.l10 // The same expression tree evaluated with a classic Visitor and with a sealed when. interface ExprVisitor<R> { fun visitNum(n: Num): R fun visitAdd(a: Add): R fun visitMul(m: Mul): R } sealed interface Expr { fun <R> accept(v: ExprVisitor<R>): R } data class Num(val value: Int) : Expr { override fun <R> accept(v: ExprVisitor<R>) = v.visitNum(this) } data class Add(val l: Expr, val r: Expr) : Expr { override fun <R> accept(v: ExprVisitor<R>) = v.visitAdd(this) } data class Mul(val l: Expr, val r: Expr) : Expr { override fun <R> accept(v: ExprVisitor<R>) = v.visitMul(this) } // operation 1, visitor style: one class per operation, one method per case object Eval : ExprVisitor<Int> { override fun visitNum(n: Num) = n.value override fun visitAdd(a: Add) = a.l.accept(this) + a.r.accept(this) override fun visitMul(m: Mul) = m.l.accept(this) * m.r.accept(this) } // operation 1 again, data style: no accept needed, no visitor interface private fun eval(e: Expr): Int = when (e) { is Num -> e.value is Add -> eval(e.l) + eval(e.r) is Mul if e.l == Num(0) -> 0 // no nested patterns in Kotlin: a guard says it is Mul -> eval(e.l) * eval(e.r) } // operation 2: just one more function private fun show(e: Expr): String = when (e) { is Num -> e.value.toString() is Add -> "(${show(e.l)} + ${show(e.r)})" is Mul -> "${show(e.l)} * ${show(e.r)}" } fun main() { val e = Add(Num(2), Mul(Num(3), Num(4))) println("${show(e)} = ${e.accept(Eval)} (visitor) = ${eval(e)} (when)") val zero = Mul(Num(0), e) println("${show(zero)} = ${eval(zero)}") }

try.expect: Both print (2 + 3 * 4) = 14 from the visitor and from the switch, then 0 * (2 + 3 * 4) = 0. Kotlin lists all three errors at once: unresolved reference 'visitNeg' and 'when' expression must be exhaustive. Add the 'is Neg' branch twice. javac reports them in rounds: cannot find symbol first; add visitNeg to ExprVisitor and you get Eval is not abstract and does not override abstract method visitNeg(Neg); implement that and the two switches fail with does not cover all possible input values. Visitor style cost the interface, accept and every visitor; switch style cost one branch per function.

sections.h: Iterator: let Kotlin write the state machine
sections.html:
Listing every refund from a PSP means walking a cursor-paginated API: fetch a page, hand out its items, follow the next cursor, stop when it's null. Loading every page into a list first wastes memory and makes the first item wait for the last page. An iterator hands them out one at a time. In Java you write its state machine by hand:

Java
static Iterator<String> refunds(Function<Integer, RefundPage> fetch) {
    return new Iterator<>() {
        private Iterator<String> current = Collections.emptyIterator();
        private Integer cursor = 0;                              // null = no more pages

        public boolean hasNext() {
            while (!current.hasNext() && cursor != null) {       // while, not if: skip empty pages
                RefundPage page = fetch.apply(cursor);
                current = page.items().iterator();
                cursor = page.next();
            }
            return current.hasNext();
        }

        public String next() {
            if (!hasNext()) throw new NoSuchElementException();
            return current.next();
        }
    };
}
Kotlin
fun refunds(fetch: (Int) -> RefundPage): Sequence<String> = sequence {
    var cursor: Int? = 0
    while (cursor != null) {
        val page = fetch(cursor)                                 // runs only when the consumer needs more
        yieldAll(page.items)
        cursor = page.next
    }
}

The Java version keeps two fields of state, and hasNext holds a classic bug: write if instead of while and an empty page in the middle ends the iteration early. Kotlin's sequence {} builder lets you write the loop you'd write for a list. yield and yieldAll suspend the block until the consumer asks for the next item, and the compiler builds the state machine. Nothing runs until someone iterates, and refunds(fetch).take(2).toList() fetches one page.

Remember two properties. A sequence built this way is cold: each new iteration runs the block again from the top, so iterating twice fetches every page twice. And if the consumer stops early, the rest of the block never runs. The iterator {} docs warn that "finally blocks may be left unexecuted". Don't open a connection inside the block and close it in finally; open it at the call site with use {}.

When you want your own type to work in a for loop, make it Iterable and build its iterator with iterator {}, the sibling of sequence {}: class RefundLog(...) : Iterable<String> { override fun iterator() = iterator { yieldAll(...) } }.

Java has no generators. Stream.iterate(seed, hasNext, next) covers simple cases, but for paging, the hand-written iterator is still the clearest Java.

try.title: Count the page fetches
steps: Run PagingDemo.kt (or its Java twin, PagingDemoJava). Before you run, predict how many GET lines each of the two calls prints.
Kotlin: change take(2) to take(3) and predict the number of GETs. Java: in hasNext, change while to if and predict the all: line.

code.title: PagingDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.patterns.l10 // Walk a cursor-paginated refunds API lazily. The sequence builder writes the iterator's state machine. data class RefundPage(val items: List<String>, val next: Int?) private val refundPages = mapOf( 0 to RefundPage(listOf("rf_1", "rf_2"), 1), 1 to RefundPage(emptyList(), 2), // an empty page in the middle 2 to RefundPage(listOf("rf_3"), null), ) fun refunds(fetch: (Int) -> RefundPage): Sequence<String> = sequence { var cursor: Int? = 0 while (cursor != null) { val page = fetch(cursor) // runs only when the consumer needs more yieldAll(page.items) cursor = page.next } } fun main() { val fetchPage = { cursor: Int -> println(" GET /refunds?cursor=$cursor"); refundPages.getValue(cursor) } println("first two: ${refunds(fetchPage).take(2).toList()}") println("all: ${refunds(fetchPage).toList()}") }

alt.title: PagingDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.patterns.l10; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.Collections; import java.util.Iterator; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.NoSuchElementException; import java.util.function.Function; /** Walk a cursor-paginated refunds API lazily. Java has no generators, so the iterator's state is written by hand. */ public class PagingDemoJava { record RefundPage(List<String> items, Integer next) {} static final Map<Integer, RefundPage> PAGES = Map.of( 0, new RefundPage(List.of("rf_1", "rf_2"), 1), 1, new RefundPage(List.of(), 2), // an empty page in the middle 2, new RefundPage(List.of("rf_3"), null)); static Iterator<String> refunds(Function<Integer, RefundPage> fetch) { return new Iterator<>() { private Iterator<String> current = Collections.emptyIterator(); private Integer cursor = 0; // null = no more pages @Override public boolean hasNext() { while (!current.hasNext() && cursor != null) { // while, not if: skip empty pages RefundPage page = fetch.apply(cursor); current = page.items().iterator(); cursor = page.next(); } return current.hasNext(); } @Override public String next() { if (!hasNext()) throw new NoSuchElementException(); return current.next(); } }; } static List<String> take(Iterator<String> it, int n) { List<String> out = new ArrayList<>(); while (out.size() < n && it.hasNext()) out.add(it.next()); return out; } public static void main(String[] args) { Function<Integer, RefundPage> fetchPage = cursor -> { System.out.println(" GET /refunds?cursor=" + cursor); return PAGES.get(cursor); }; System.out.println("first two: " + take(refunds(fetchPage), 2)); System.out.println("all: " + take(refunds(fetchPage), Integer.MAX_VALUE)); } }

try.expect: first two: fetches only page 0; all: fetches pages 0, 1 and 2 and prints [rf_1, rf_2, rf_3]. With take(3), three GETs run, because the third item sits behind the empty page. With if in Java, the iterator fetches the empty page, finds nothing and gives up: all: [rf_1, rf_2] after two GETs, and rf_3 is silently lost.

sections.h: Memento: a snapshot you can hand back
sections.html:
An analyst editing a draft refund batch adds lines, sets a note, then wants to undo. Observer and Command undid a command by running its inverse. That works for "add 30". It doesn't for "apply the discount rules", which has no clean inverse. Memento saves a snapshot of the state before the change and puts it back on undo:

Java
final class Cart {
    private final List<String> items = new ArrayList<>();
    private String coupon = "";

    interface Memento {}                                             // what callers hold: opaque
    private record State(List<String> items, String coupon) implements Memento {}

    Memento save() { return new State(List.copyOf(items), coupon); } // copy: later edits must not leak in

    void restore(Memento m) {
        State s = (State) m;
        items.clear();
        items.addAll(s.items());                                     // copy back in: the memento stays intact
        coupon = s.coupon();
    }
}
Kotlin
class Cart {
    private val items = mutableListOf<String>()
    private var coupon = ""

    interface Memento                                                // what callers hold: opaque
    private data class State(val items: List<String>, val coupon: String) : Memento

    fun save(): Memento = State(items.toList(), coupon)             // copy: later edits must not leak in

    fun restore(m: Memento) {
        val s = m as State
        items.clear()
        items += s.items                                             // copy back in: the memento stays intact
        coupon = s.coupon
    }
}

Three rules make it work. The snapshot must not share mutable parts with the live object: copy the list with List.copyOf or toList(), or later edits leak into the saved state. Restore must copy back in rather than point at the memento's list, so the same memento can be restored twice. And only the originator reads it. Callers get an opaque Memento to store and hand back, while the record with the data is private, so nothing else depends on the cart's insides.

When the whole state is already an immutable record or data class, the pattern almost disappears: the state is its own memento, and an undo history is a List<State>. That is a strong argument for immutable aggregates.

There are two costs. History grows with every checkpoint, so bound it; the lab keeps the newest N. And snapshots of large aggregates are expensive, which is why event-sourced systems store one every few hundred events and replay the rest.

try.title: Let the snapshot share the list
steps: Run MementoDemo in either language and read both lines.
In save(), store the live list instead of a copy: new State(items, coupon) in Java, State(items, coupon) in Kotlin. Predict the restored: line, then run.

code.title: MementoDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.patterns.l10; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** A cart that can hand out a snapshot of itself and later put it back. */ public class MementoDemo { static final class Cart { private final List<String> items = new ArrayList<>(); private String coupon = ""; void add(String item) { items.add(item); } void coupon(String code) { coupon = code; } @Override public String toString() { return items + " coupon=" + coupon; } // callers see an opaque Memento; only Cart can read the State inside it interface Memento {} private record State(List<String> items, String coupon) implements Memento {} Memento save() { return new State(List.copyOf(items), coupon); // copy: later edits must not leak in } void restore(Memento m) { State s = (State) m; items.clear(); items.addAll(s.items()); // copy back in: the memento stays as it was coupon = s.coupon(); } } public static void main(String[] args) { Cart cart = new Cart(); cart.add("sku-1"); Cart.Memento before = cart.save(); cart.add("sku-2"); cart.coupon("AUTUMN10"); System.out.println("edited: " + cart); cart.restore(before); System.out.println("restored: " + cart); } }

alt.title: MementoDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.patterns.l10 // A cart that can hand out a snapshot of itself and later put it back. class Cart { private val items = mutableListOf<String>() private var coupon = "" fun add(item: String) { items += item } fun coupon(code: String) { coupon = code } override fun toString() = "$items coupon=$coupon" // callers see an opaque Memento; only Cart can read the State inside it interface Memento private data class State(val items: List<String>, val coupon: String) : Memento fun save(): Memento = State(items.toList(), coupon) // copy: later edits must not leak in fun restore(m: Memento) { val s = m as State items.clear() items += s.items // copy back in: the memento stays as it was coupon = s.coupon } } fun main() { val cart = Cart() cart.add("sku-1") val before = cart.save() cart.add("sku-2") cart.coupon("AUTUMN10") println("edited: $cart") cart.restore(before) println("restored: $cart") }

try.expect: edited: [sku-1, sku-2] coupon=AUTUMN10, then restored: [sku-1] coupon=. Without the copy, the memento and the cart share one list. sku-2 lands in the "saved" state too, and restore then clears that shared list before copying from it, so you get restored: [] coupon=: worse than no undo at all.

sections.html:
A checkout touches inventory, payments, shipping and email, and each reacts to the others: missing stock means a refund, a captured payment means ship and send a receipt. If every service calls the ones it reacts to, four services need six links, and every new rule edits two of them. A mediator owns the coordination, and each colleague talks only to it:

Java
interface Colleague { void receive(String event); }

final class CheckoutMediator {
    private final Map<String, List<Colleague>> routes = new HashMap<>();
    void on(String event, Colleague c) { routes.computeIfAbsent(event, k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(c); }
    void emit(String event) { routes.getOrDefault(event, List.of()).forEach(c -> c.receive(event)); }
}

mediator.on("payment.captured", shipping);
mediator.on("payment.captured", email);
mediator.on("stock.missing", payments);        // payments refunds; inventory never calls payments directly
Kotlin
fun interface Colleague { fun receive(event: String) }

class CheckoutMediator {
    private val routes = mutableMapOf<String, MutableList<Colleague>>()
    fun on(event: String, c: Colleague) { routes.getOrPut(event) { mutableListOf() } += c }
    fun emit(event: String) { routes[event].orEmpty().forEach { it.receive(event) } }
}

mediator.on("payment.captured", shipping)
mediator.on("payment.captured", email)
mediator.on("stock.missing", payments)         // payments refunds; inventory never calls payments directly

Mediator and Observer look alike. An observer is one subject telling many listeners about itself. A mediator sits between many parties and holds the rules about who reacts to what. In coroutine code, a MutableSharedFlow<CheckoutEvent> that all colleagues share is a natural mediator bus. Across services, the mediator becomes a message broker or a saga orchestrator: a Temporal workflow that calls the inventory, payment and shipping activities in order is a mediator with durable state.

The risk is the god object. A mediator should route and sequence. When it starts computing fees or validating addresses, move that logic back to the colleague that owns it.

the rules live in one place</text></svg>
figure.caption: Without a mediator every service knows the others. With one, each knows only the hub, and the coordination rules live in one place.

analogy: A visitor is a tax inspector who visits every kind of business with a different checklist for each; a new kind of business means every inspector learns a new checklist. An iterator is a librarian fetching books one at a time from the stacks, so you can start reading before the last shelf is reached. A memento is a photo of a whiteboard before you erase it. A mediator is an air-traffic tower: planes talk to the tower, never to each other. The analogy breaks on the photo. A photo can't change after you take it, but a software memento that shares a list with the live object changes every time you edit, which is the bug the lesson's demo shows.
world: The PSP clients in your services almost certainly page: refunds, disputes, payouts, settlement lines. Expose each as a Kotlin Sequence (or a Java Iterator) that fetches lazily, and the reconciliation job can stop at the first mismatch without downloading the rest. Mind that iterating twice hits the API twice. Memento is how a back-office tool offers undo on a draft refund batch, and how an event-sourced ledger keeps snapshots so that replay stays fast. Mediator is your checkout orchestration: inside one Quarkus service it can be a small router or a shared flow, and across services it is the Temporal workflow that sequences inventory, payment and shipping activities. Visitor shows up mostly when you write annotation processors or bytecode tools; in your own domain code, sealed types and switch or when replace it.
mistake: The most common Memento mistake is a shallow snapshot: save() stores a reference to the object's live mutable list (or an array, or a mutable nested object) instead of a copy. It happens because records and data classes look immutable, so new State(items, coupon) feels like a snapshot. It isn't: the record holds the same list the object keeps editing, so the "saved" state changes with every edit, and undo restores the present instead of the past. Copy every mutable part when you save (List.copyOf, toList()), copy again when you restore, and test it the way the lab does: save, edit, restore, edit again, restore again.

compare.title: Replacing a visitor: nested patterns in Java, guards in Kotlin

java.title: Expr.java
java.html: sealed interface Expr permits Num, Add, Mul {} record Num(int value) implements Expr {} record Add(Expr left, Expr right) implements Expr {} record Mul(Expr left, Expr right) implements Expr {} static int eval(Expr e) { return switch (e) { case Num(var v) -> v; case Add(var l, var r) -> eval(l) + eval(r); case Mul(Num(var z), var r) when z == 0 -> 0; // nested record pattern: skip the right side case Mul(var l, var r) -> eval(l) * eval(r); }; } static String show(Expr e) { // a new operation: one new function, no class touched return switch (e) { case Num(var v) -> Integer.toString(v); case Add(var l, var r) -> "(" + show(l) + " + " + show(r) + ")"; case Mul(var l, var r) -> show(l) + " * " + show(r); }; }

kotlin.title: Expr.kt
kotlin.html: sealed interface Expr data class Num(val value: Int) : Expr data class Add(val left: Expr, val right: Expr) : Expr data class Mul(val left: Expr, val right: Expr) : Expr fun eval(e: Expr): Int = when (e) { is Num -> e.value is Add -> eval(e.left) + eval(e.right) is Mul if e.left == Num(0) -> 0 // no nested patterns in Kotlin: a guard says it is Mul -> eval(e.left) * eval(e.right) } fun show(e: Expr): String = when (e) { // a new operation: one new function, no class touched is Num -> e.value.toString() is Add -> "(${show(e.left)} + ${show(e.right)})" is Mul -> "${show(e.left)} * ${show(e.right)}" }

compare.note: Both delete the visitor interface and every accept method, and both make a new operation a single function. The difference is how far the patterns reach. Java 21 record patterns nest, so Mul(Num(var z), var r) when z == 0 matches "a multiplication whose left side is the literal 0" in one case, and binds the fields as it goes. Kotlin's when matches on type and smart-casts, but has no destructuring patterns, so the same rule is a guard (is Mul if e.left == Num(0)), which works because data classes compare by value. Guards in when are stable since Kotlin 2.2.0. In both, adding a case such as Neg breaks every function that switches over Expr, which is the compiler listing your work.

worked.title: Retire a visitor in four steps

steps.say: A fee-formula engine evaluates and prints expressions with a classic visitor. Product wants negation. Before reading on, list every file a Neg node touches in this design.
steps.code: interface ExprVisitor<R> { R visitNum(Num n); R visitAdd(Add a); R visitMul(Mul m); } sealed interface Expr permits Num, Add, Mul { <R> R accept(ExprVisitor<R> v); } // Num, Add, Mul: each record implements accept(v) by calling its own visitXxx(this) final class Eval implements ExprVisitor<Integer> { /* three visit methods */ } final class Show implements ExprVisitor<String> { /* three visit methods */ } // ...and any visitor another team wrote against ExprVisitor

alt.html: interface ExprVisitor<R> { fun visitNum(n: Num): R; fun visitAdd(a: Add): R; fun visitMul(m: Mul): R } sealed interface Expr { fun <R> accept(v: ExprVisitor<R>): R } // Num, Add, Mul: each data class implements accept(v) by calling its own visitXxx(this) object Eval : ExprVisitor<Int> { /* three visit methods */ } object Show : ExprVisitor<String> { /* three visit methods */ } // ...and any visitor another team wrote against ExprVisitor

steps.say: Neg needs a visitNeg on the interface, an accept on itself, and a new method in Eval, Show and every other visitor. The hierarchy is closed and ours, so retire the machinery first: drop accept and the interface, and write each operation as a switch. Behavior doesn't change; run the old tests.
steps.code: sealed interface Expr permits Num, Add, Mul {} // 1. no accept, no visitor interface record Num(int value) implements Expr {} record Add(Expr left, Expr right) implements Expr {} record Mul(Expr left, Expr right) implements Expr {} static int eval(Expr e) { // 2. each visitor becomes one function return switch (e) { case Num(var v) -> v; case Add(var l, var r) -> eval(l) + eval(r); case Mul(var l, var r) -> eval(l) * eval(r); }; }

alt.html: sealed interface Expr // 1. no accept, no visitor interface data class Num(val value: Int) : Expr data class Add(val left: Expr, val right: Expr) : Expr data class Mul(val left: Expr, val right: Expr) : Expr fun eval(e: Expr): Int = when (e) { // 2. each visitor becomes one function is Num -> e.value is Add -> eval(e.left) + eval(e.right) is Mul -> eval(e.left) * eval(e.right) }

steps.say: Now add the case, and compile before writing any logic. The errors are the to-do list: one per function that switches over Expr.
steps.code: sealed interface Expr permits Num, Add, Mul, Neg {} record Neg(Expr e) implements Expr {} // 3. the new case // javac: error: the switch expression does not cover all possible input values (eval) // javac: error: the switch expression does not cover all possible input values (show)

alt.html: data class Neg(val e: Expr) : Expr // 3. the new case // kotlinc: 'when' expression must be exhaustive. Add the 'is Neg' branch or an 'else' branch. (eval) // kotlinc: 'when' expression must be exhaustive. Add the 'is Neg' branch or an 'else' branch. (show)

steps.say: Fill in one branch per function. A brand-new operation, counting nodes for a complexity limit, is one more function, and no type changes at all.
steps.code: case Neg(var x) -> -eval(x); // 4. in eval case Neg(var x) -> "-" + show(x); // in show static int count(Expr e) { // 5. a new operation: one function return switch (e) { case Num n -> 1; case Add(var l, var r) -> 1 + count(l) + count(r); case Mul(var l, var r) -> 1 + count(l) + count(r); case Neg(var x) -> 1 + count(x); }; }

alt.html: is Neg -> -eval(e.e) // 4. in eval is Neg -> "-${show(e.e)}" // in show fun count(e: Expr): Int = when (e) { // 5. a new operation: one function is Num -> 1 is Add -> 1 + count(e.left) + count(e.right) is Mul -> 1 + count(e.left) + count(e.right) is Neg -> 1 + count(e.e) }

lab.title: A lazy paging sequence and an invoice draft with undo
steps: Run the tests once: all nine fail.
In Paging.kt, write pagedSequence with the sequence {} builder: start at cursor 0, fetch a page, hand out its items, follow next until it is null.

In InvoiceDraft, add a private data class that implements Memento and holds the lines and the note. save() stores copies; restore checks the type with require, then copies the lines back into the draft's own list.
Write DraftHistory: keep mementos in an ArrayDeque, drop the oldest when there are more than limit, and restore the newest on undo.
Run the tests until all nine pass. Then read the test that restores the same memento twice, and say which line of your restore makes it pass.
hints: Inside sequence {}, an ordinary while loop and yieldAll(page.items) are all you need. An empty page yields nothing, and the loop carries on to the next cursor.
After require(m is State) { "..." }, Kotlin smart-casts m to State for the rest of the function. A private nested class may implement a public nested interface.
In restore, lines.clear() then lines.addAll(m.lines) keeps the memento's list untouched. Assigning the memento's list to the draft instead would let the next edit change the memento.

drill.title: A paging iterator in Java, from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write the Java version: static Iterator<String> refunds(Function<Integer, RefundPage> fetch), where RefundPage(List<String> items, Integer next) and next is null on the last page. It must skip empty pages and fetch nothing until hasNext is called. Then write the Kotlin sequence {} version and compare how much state each one keeps.

answer.html: static Iterator<String> refunds(Function<Integer, RefundPage> fetch) { return new Iterator<>() { private Iterator<String> current = Collections.emptyIterator(); private Integer cursor = 0; // null = no more pages @Override public boolean hasNext() { while (!current.hasNext() && cursor != null) { // while, not if: skip empty pages RefundPage page = fetch.apply(cursor); current = page.items().iterator(); cursor = page.next(); } return current.hasNext(); } @Override public String next() { if (!hasNext()) throw new NoSuchElementException(); return current.next(); } }; }

alt.title: Kotlin
alt.html: fun refunds(fetch: (Int) -> RefundPage): Sequence<String> = sequence { var cursor: Int? = 0 // the only state you write while (cursor != null) { val page = fetch(cursor) yieldAll(page.items) // an empty page yields nothing cursor = page.next } }

recap: The expression problem: virtual methods make new cases cheap, Visitor makes new operations cheap. Sealed types plus switch or when give Visitor's side with no accept and no visitor interface.
Delete visitors for closed hierarchies you own. Keep Visitor for open hierarchies or library APIs, such as annotation processing and bytecode tools.
Kotlin's sequence {} turns a plain loop into a lazy iterator. Java needs a hand-written Iterator, with while, not if, in hasNext.
A built sequence is cold (iterating again reruns the block) and may stop early, so finally inside it may never run.
Memento: save a private, immutable snapshot that copies every mutable part, restore by copying back in, and bound the history.
Mediator: colleagues talk only to a hub that holds the coordination rules. Keep it to routing and sequencing.

explain.prompt: A teammate wants to add a Visitor to the sealed PaymentInstruction hierarchy "so we can add operations without touching the classes". Explain what you would do instead, and when you would agree with them.
explain.answer: We own the hierarchy and it's sealed, so we already get what a visitor gives: we can add an operation without touching the records by writing one function with a switch (or when) over the five types. The compiler checks that each function covers every type, and record patterns let us match nested shapes that a visitor can't express easily. A visitor would add an interface with five methods and an accept on every record, and nothing else. The cost is the same either way when a new instruction type arrives: every operation must handle it, but with sealed types the compiler lists each one. I'd agree to a visitor if the hierarchy were open to other modules we can't recompile, or if we were plugging into a library that already speaks visitors, such as an annotation processor.

deeper.html:
Kotlin's sequence {} is built on the same machinery as coroutines, but restricted. Its block runs on a SequenceScope, which allows only yield and yieldAll to suspend, so you can't call delay or another suspend function inside it. For asynchronous paging, where each page fetch is itself a suspending HTTP call, use flow {} and emit instead: a Flow is the suspending cousin of a sequence, cold in the same way, and covered in the coroutines track.

Java's Iterator has an optional remove(), and its Javadoc says iterators "allow the caller to remove elements from the underlying collection during the iteration with well-defined semantics". That's why iterator.remove() is safe inside a loop where list.remove(x) throws ConcurrentModificationException. For paging iterators, leave remove() unsupported, which is the default.

Visitor and Composite often travel together: a visitor walks a composite tree. With sealed types, the walk is just recursion in each function, as in Composite, Bridge and Flyweight. If trees get deep enough to overflow the stack, an explicit stack in an iterator (or a sequence {} that pushes children) turns the recursion into iteration.

Memento meets event sourcing in snapshots. An aggregate's state is the fold of its events. Replaying ten thousand events on every load is slow, so the store keeps a snapshot every few hundred events, and loading means restoring the newest snapshot and replaying what came after it. The snapshot format then becomes a contract between versions of your code, so give it a version field from the start.
